name: Height fraud (footwear and lifts)

lead: Height fraud means using footwear modifications to look taller than your barefoot height. The usual tools are removable heel lifts, full insoles and shoes with thick or hidden-lift soles. Elevator shoes place the raised section inside the shoe so it is not obvious to observers, unlike visible high heels [1].

On looksmax.org, height is treated as a major factor in how people are perceived, so lifts are a popular low-cost way to gain a few centimetres immediately. Posters share which shoes hide lifts best and how much extra height can pass unnoticed.

paras: Community guides describe choosing high-top shoes or boots that grip the heel, using one-inch or larger insoles, and stacking them under the original sole so the lift is hidden [2][3]. One poster notes that a lift advertised at 2.5 inches adds less effective height because the forefoot rises far less than the heel [4]. Many posters pair lifts with a claimed height a little under the lifted total.

Posters and guides mention discomfort, an altered walk and possible spine or foot strain with large lifts, and social embarrassment if the lifts are noticed. No published trial has studied looksmaxxing-style lift use.

angle.text: Concealed lifts add height as long as they are worn. Community guides describe the gain as less than the advertised lift thickness because of the heel-to-toe slope.

lead: Height fraud, also written heightfraud, is community slang on looksmax.org for appearing taller with concealed footwear aids such as shoe lifts, insoles and thick-soled shoes. The practice is a direct way to add height while worn: the lift raises the heel and, to a lesser degree, the front of the foot [1].

Elevator shoes are a long-standing product category in which the height-adding component sits inside the shoe so observers cannot see it, and which may be made of plastic, wood or rubber [2]. Forum guides build on this idea with advice about shoe styles, hiding methods and the height to state [3][4].
Posters debate how much can be added before it is noticeable or uncomfortable. Claims in threads range from about one inch to over three inches [3][1].

paras: Elevator shoes have thickened sections under the heels, called shoe lifts, that raise apparent height. Because the raised part is inside the shoe, observers do not see it, in contrast to high-heeled shoes [2]. Shoes with thickened soles are also used for orthopaedic reasons, although the term elevator shoe usually does not apply to those [2].

Looksmax.org members post guides on the subject. One poster who describes wearing roughly 3.5 inches of lift for two years explains that lifts do not behave like standing on a brick, because the front of the foot rises much less than the heel, so a lift advertised at 2.5 inches adds closer to 1.5 inches by the poster's own measurement [1]. Another guide recommends common high-top shoes and boots, insoles of about one inch, hiding the lift under the original insole, and choosing a claimed height that is believable [3].

Other threads ask which shoes accommodate lifts discreetly [4] and discuss shoes with built-in lift for formal wear [5]. Commenters describe concealment from partners and acquaintances as a main concern [3][1].

Guides themselves caution that overly large lifts can produce an unusual walk and strain [3]. Beyond forum commentary, no medical source examined here assesses cosmetic lift use. Social risk, being discovered wearing lifts, is a recurring theme in threads [3][1].

lore.intro: Height fraud is a staple topic on looksmax.org, where members trade shoe recommendations and concealment tactics [3][4][1].
